children.text: The National Shrine of Our Lady of La Naval de Manila on Quezon Avenue in Quezon City is a large Art Deco-style church that the Dominicans rebuilt in the 1950s. Its huge stained-glass windows, murals and ivory image of the Virgin are the highlights, and it was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2012.

Santo Domingo Church is formally called the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Holy Rosary of La Naval de Manila, and it stands at 537 Quezon Avenue in Quezon City, Metro Manila. Locals simply call it "Santo Domingo." It belongs to the Diocese of Cubao and is run by Dominican (Order of Preachers) priests. For travelers, it is a chance to see a large mid-20th-century church that looks very different from the old churches of Intramuros in central Manila.

The church traces its roots to 1587. The Dominicans, who arrived in Manila from Cádiz, Spain, founded it that year, and the first church, built of light materials, was inaugurated on January 1, 1588. It was destroyed several times by earthquakes and fires, and the fifth church in Intramuros, a neo-Gothic building built from 1864 to 1887, was destroyed in late December 1941 at the start of World War II. The current sixth church broke ground in 1952 and was consecrated in 1954; sources record the date as either October 10 or 12. After the Intramuros church was lost, the faithful saved the Marian image and kept it for a time in the Santísimo Rosario Church at the University of Santo Tomas, and it is said to have been brought here in procession once the new church was built. The church is still regarded as the heir to the memory of the old Intramuros church.

The architect was José María Zaragoza, who is said to have designed the church while still an architecture student at the University of Santo Tomas. It is a cruciform reinforced-concrete building about 85 m long, 40 m wide and 25 m high, combining Art Deco and Spanish Modern styles with Mission, Romanesque and Gothic elements. The facade carries a high-relief frieze telling the story of the La Naval de Manila naval battles, and inside you will find murals by National Artist Carlos Francisco and stained glass designed by Galo Ocampo. Stepping in, you see a wide, high-ceilinged space with few columns, a design said to leave the decoration to the murals, glass and reliefs while the building itself keeps large, simple lines. A single walk-through takes about an hour, but allow around two hours if you want to read each window and mural.

The spiritual heart of the church is the image of Our Lady of La Naval. In 1646 the Manila defenders won five naval battles against the Dutch fleet, a victory credited to the help of Our Lady of the Rosary, and she was given the title "La Naval" (the naval battle). The image was canonically crowned on October 5, 1907, and was proclaimed patroness of Quezon City in 1973. In 2012 the church was declared a National Cultural Treasure.

blocks.title: Art Deco facade and high relief

children.text: The receding planes of the facade, the corbel arches and the high-relief frieze of the La Naval battle above the three portals are striking. The best photo spot is the front plaza on the Quezon Avenue side. The building is about 25 m high, which feels imposing up close, while from a distance its linear Art Deco outline stands out clearly.

The windows, designed by Galo Ocampo, depict the Fifteen Mysteries of the Rosary, the Battles of Lepanto and La Naval, and the stories of martyred saints. When sunlight comes in between morning and midday, the church fills with color. Each window has a different theme, so it helps to read any posted explanation as you walk around.

The nave walls hold eight murals on the life of Saint Dominic by Philippine National Artist Carlos Francisco. The murals of the Four Evangelists by Antonio García Llamas are painted in calm brown tones.

Large bas-reliefs of Saint Dominic by the Italian sculptor Francesco (Riccardo) Monti decorate the facade and the base of the belfry. As befits a Dominican church, the founder of the order is honored prominently.

blocks.title: Image of Our Lady of La Naval

children.text: This ivory image of Our Lady of the Rosary is kept on the left side altar for most of the year. During the October feast it is said to be moved under a canopy behind the main altar, so check on site where it is enthroned during your visit. Access may be limited during the feast or special events, so follow the instructions on site.

The museum to the left of the church is known to display crucifixes, rosaries and a tabernacle from the Intramuros church. Opening hours may not be fixed, so it is safest to ask the parish office before you visit.

An organ built in Hong Kong by the Dominican friar Gregorio Hontomin is said to have been moved to this church in 1954 and inaugurated in 1959. It was restored by Diego Cera Organbuilders. Whether you can hear it during Mass depends on the schedule.
The church-run restaurant Cafe Inggo 1587 opened in 2017 at the southwest of the grounds. It serves Spanish and Filipino dishes and is a good place to rest before or after Mass.
Take a taxi or Grab to 537 Quezon Avenue and first look over the exterior and the high relief from the front plaza.
Enter the nave in modest clothing and look around at the stained glass and Carlos Francisco's murals. Avoid taking photos or moving around during Mass.
Spend a moment in front of the image of Our Lady of La Naval at the left side altar, and ask at the office whether the museum is open.
Rest with an early lunch at Cafe Inggo 1587.
Continue by taxi to the University of Santo Tomas or Quezon Memorial Circle.
The Mass schedule changes by day and season, so check the church's announcements before you visit.
Start in Intramuros and walk around Manila Cathedral and San Agustin Church to get a feel for the area where the Dominicans first settled.
Find the historical marker at the site of the old Santo Domingo church and take a photo. A financial building now stands there.
Have lunch, then take Grab or a taxi to Quezon Avenue.
Arrive at Santo Domingo Church, view the high relief and stained glass on the facade, and reflect on the story in front of the image of Our Lady of La Naval.
Enjoy a snack at Cafe Inggo 1587 and, if time remains, move on to a nearby Quezon City attraction.
This course takes the whole day, so keep the schedule loose to allow for Manila traffic.
From central Manila (Malate, Ermita), Grab or a taxi is the easiest and takes about
40 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes
depending on traffic.
By public transport, you can take a bus or jeepney along Quezon Avenue and get off near Santo Domingo. Routes can change, so check locally.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), Grab or a taxi takes about
1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes
when traffic is light.
MRT-3 Quezon Avenue Station is relatively close, but the church is several kilometers away in a straight line, so you need to take another taxi or tricycle after getting off.
The dry season from November to May is best for walking and sightseeing. The inside of the church is relatively cool, but the walk across the plaza is hot at midday.

Around the second Sunday of October is the La Naval feast period, when tens of thousands of people may gather. It is good if you want to see the procession and Mass, but if you want to see the architecture quietly, it is better to avoid this period.

During the day, early morning or late afternoon is quieter and less hot. Sunday mornings are crowded with Mass-goers, which makes sightseeing difficult, while weekday daytime is relatively relaxed for viewing the architecture. However, weekday Mass times may differ from what has been confirmed, so check the church's announcements before you visit.

You cannot stay overnight inside the church, so it is more practical to stay in a hotel in Quiapo, central Manila or Quezon City. There are several budget and mid-range hotels around Quezon Avenue, so check the latest ratings and rates on a map app.

The nearest place to eat is Cafe Inggo 1587 on the grounds. It is known to serve Spanish and Filipino dishes, so check the menu and opening hours before you visit. Around Quezon Avenue there are also many Filipino home-style restaurants and fast-food outlets.

Apart from the cafe on the grounds, you can try Filipino home-style dishes such as sinigang and adobo at local restaurants, or use a food court in a nearby shopping mall. If you plan a meal after visiting the church, allow plenty of travel time so it does not clash with Mass times.
Dress with your shoulders and knees covered. It is a place of worship, so take off your hat.
The center of the nave fills with worshippers during Mass, so choose a time without Mass and walk along the sides.
The parish office is known to be closed on Mondays, so visit on another day if you need to ask about the museum or other matters.
The stained glass looks most beautiful when the morning sun shines through.
Take photos inside the church quietly and without flash, and do not photograph people at prayer.
Seeing the site of the old church in Intramuros as well makes it easier to understand this church's history.
Parking and roads are very crowded during the October feast, so use public transport and walk.
Quezon Avenue in front of the church is busy with traffic, so check pedestrian signals and the location of footbridges when crossing.
Carrying small bills makes it easier to pay for donations, candles and tricycle fares.
When calling a Grab, entering the destination as "Sto. Domingo Church, Quezon Avenue" gives the exact location.
During the La Naval feast (around the second Sunday of October), crowds cause traffic jams and pickpocketing can increase.
At crowded events, carry your bag in front and watch your phone and wallet.
Mass and event schedules can change, so check the latest announcements before you visit.
Some details of the museum's opening and admission rules are unconfirmed, so check locally.
When taking a taxi, use the meter or confirm the fare in advance through Grab.
During the rainy season, showers can delay travel.
There may be street vendors and touts around the church, so politely decline unnecessary bargaining.
